en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 17.
Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Schism in the Sangha)
1. The Discourse on the Sakyan Youth’s Going Forth At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Anupiyā, a market town of the Mallas named Anupiyā.
Now at that time, many well-known Sakyan youths were going forth after the Blessed One who had himself gone forth.
Now at that time, Mahānāma the Sakyan and Anuruddha the Sakyan were two brothers.
Anuruddha the Sakyan was delicate;
he had three palaces—
One was for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.
During the four months of the rainy season, while being entertained by female musicians in the rain-palace, he did not descend from the palace.
Then, this thought occurred to Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“Now indeed, many well-known Sakyan youths are following the Blessed One who has gone forth by going forth themselves.
Yet, from our own family, no one has gone forth from the home life into homelessness.
What if either I were to go forth, or Anuruddha?”
Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached Anuruddha the Sakyan and, having approached him, said this to Anuruddha the Sakyan:
"At present, dear Anuruddha, many well-known Sakyan youths are going forth after the Blessed One who has himself gone forth.
Yet, in our own family, there is no one who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness."
“In that case, either you go forth, or I shall go forth.
“I am indeed delicate; I am not able to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
You go forth.”
“Come now, dear Anuruddha, I will instruct you in the duties of household life.
First, the fields must be plowed;
having had them plowed, they must be sown.”
Having had the hair shaved off, water should be poured over it.
Having poured water over it, the water should be drained away.
Having drained away the water, it should be cleared out.
Having had it removed, it should be winnowed.
Having had it winnowed, it should be threshed.
Having had it threshed, it should be made into a heap.
Having had it piled up, it should be threshed.
Having had it threshed, the straw should be removed.
Having had the straw removed, the chaff should be removed.
Having had the husks removed, it should be winnowed.
Having had it winnowed, it should be brought in.
Having had it brought in, it should be done exactly like this for the coming rainy season as well; it should be done exactly like this for the coming rainy season as well.”
“Do actions not exhaust?
Is no end to actions discerned?
When will actions be exhausted?”
“When will an end to our work be seen?
When shall we, free from anxiety, enjoy ourselves, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure?
“No indeed, dear Anuruddha; work does not come to an end.”
"No end to kamma is discerned;
yet while their kamma was not yet exhausted, your father and grandfather have passed away.
"In that case, you yourself should take up the life of a householder."
“I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Then Anuruddha the Sakyan approached his mother; having approached her, he said this to his mother:
“Mother, I wish to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“Give me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
When this was said, Anuruddha the Sakyan’s mother said this to him:
“My dear Anuruddha, you two sons are dear and pleasing to me, never disagreeable.”
“Even by death shall I be separated from you against your will.
How then could I permit you, while you are still living, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?
A second time also... [and so on].
A third time, Anuruddha the Sakyan said this to his mother:
“Mother, I wish to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Please give me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
Now at that time, Bhaddiya the Sakyan king was ruling over the Sakyans,
and he was a friend of Anuruddha the Sakyan. Then Anuruddha’s mother—
“This Bhaddiya, the Sakyan king, rules over the kingdom of the Sakyans;
he is a friend of Anuruddha the Sakyan,
and he does not venture to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
He said this to Anuruddha the Sakyan:
“Dear Anuruddha, if Bhaddiya the Sakyan king goes forth from the home life into homelessness, then you too should go forth.
Then Anuruddha the Sakyan approached Bhaddiya the Sakyan king; having approached him, he said this to Bhaddiya the Sakyan king:
“Friend, my going forth depends on you.
“Friend, whether your going forth depends on me or not, let it be so;
go forth as you please with me.”
“Come, friend, let us both go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Friend, I am not able to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Whatever else you can have me do, I shall do that; what can I do?”
“You should go forth.
“My mother, friend, said this to me:
‘If, dear Anuruddha, Bhaddiya the Sakyan king goes forth from the home life into homelessness, then you too should go forth.’”
“Indeed, friend, those words were spoken by you.
Whether your going forth depends on me or does not depend on me, friend,
go forth as you please.”
“Come, friend, let us both go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Now at that time, people were speakers of truth and true to their word.
Then Bhaddiya the Sakyan king said this to Anuruddha the Sakyan:
“Come, friend, wait seven years.
After the passing of seven years, we both shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Seven years, friend, is far too long.”
“I cannot wait for seven years.
“Wait, friend, for six years … five years …”
four years … three years … two years …
“One year.
At the end of one year, we both shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“A year is too long, friend.”
“I cannot wait for even one year.
“Wait, friend, for seven months.
At the end of seven months, we both shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“Seven months is far too long, friend;
I cannot wait for seven months.
“Wait, friend, for six months…” [and so on].
For five months...
for four months...
for three months...
For two months … for one month … for half a month.
“At the end of half a month, we both shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Half a month is too long, friend;
I cannot wait for half a month.”
“Wait, friend, for seven days until I hand over the kingdom to my sons and brothers.
“It will not be long, friend; we shall wait for seven days.
Then Bhaddiya the Sakyan king, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila, and Devadatta—
And with Upāli the barber as the seventh, just as they used to go out to the park grounds in a fourfold army in the past,
so too did they set out with a fourfold army.

Having gone a great distance, they turned back the army, entered a foreign territory, removed their ornaments, tied their belongings in a bundle with their upper robes, and said this to Upāli the barber:
“Come now, friend Upāli, turn back;
this much is enough for your livelihood.
Then, as the barber Upāli was turning back, this thought occurred to him:
“The Sakyans are indeed fierce;
thinking, ‘He has sent these princes away,’ they might even have me executed.
For these very Sakyan princes are about to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
“What then of me? Releasing his bundle and hanging that merchandise on a tree, he said, “Whoever sees it, let him take what has been given,” and approached those Sakyan youths.
Those Sakyan youths saw the barber Upāli coming from afar.
Having seen him, they said this to Upāli the barber:
“Why, my dear Upāli, have you turned back?
“Just now, noble sirs, as I was turning back, this thought occurred to me:”
"The Śākyans are indeed fierce;
thinking, 'He has caused our princes to be expelled,' they might even have me executed.
For these very Śākya princes will go forth from the home into homelessness."
"And why, then? "Because, noble sirs, having untied my bundle and hung that merchandise on a tree, I said, 'Whoever sees it, let him take what is given,' and then I turned back.
"Very well, Upāli, you did right not to turn back," he said.
“The Śākyans are fierce;
thinking, ‘These youths have been dismissed by this man,’ they might even have him executed.
Then the Śākyan youths, taking Upāli the barber with them, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting to one side, those Sakyan youths said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, we Sakyans are indeed proud.
This barber Upāli, venerable sir, has been our attendant for a long time."
"Let the Blessed One ordain him first.
We shall perform for him acts of salutation, rising from our seats, joining our palms, and respectful homage.
In this way, the pride of us Sakyans will be humbled."
Then the Blessed One first gave the going-forth to Upāli the barber, and afterwards to those Sakyan princes.
Then, within that very same rainy season, the Venerable Bhaddiya realized the threefold knowledge;
the Venerable Anuruddha produced the divine eye.
The Venerable Ānanda realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Devadatta manifested mundane psychic power.
Now at that time, the Venerable Bhaddiya, whether gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty hut, frequently uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, whenever the Venerable Bhaddiya goes to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he frequently utters this inspired exclamation:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
Without a doubt, venerable sir, the Venerable Bhaddiya is practicing the holy life without finding delight in it.”
Or, recollecting that very same former happiness of kingship, even when he had gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he would frequently utter this inspired exclamation:
“Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, in my name address the bhikkhu Bhaddiya, saying:
‘Friend Bhaddiya, the Teacher calls you.
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One, and he approached the Venerable Bhaddiya and said this to him:
“The Teacher calls you, friend Bhaddiya.
“Very well, friend,” the Venerable Bhaddiya replied to that bhikkhu, and he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Bhaddiya was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Is it true, Bhaddiya, that even when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, you frequently utter this inspired exclamation:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’?
“It is so, Bhante.”
“But what benefit, Bhaddiya, do you see that, even when gone to the forest, gone to the foot of a tree, or gone to an empty hut, you frequently utter this inspired utterance:
‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’?
“Formerly, venerable sir, while I was a king, protection was well-arranged for me both inside and outside the inner palace.”
Protection is well-arranged; protection is well-arranged both within the city and outside the city, and protection is well-arranged both within the countryside and outside the countryside.
Yet, venerable sir, even though I am thus protected and guarded, I dwell afraid, anxious, apprehensive, and terrified.
"But now, Bhante, whether I have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, I dwell alone—
fearless, undismayed, unsuspecting, unafraid, unconcerned, with hair on end, subsisting on what others give, with a mind like that of a deer.
It is seeing this purpose, Bhante, that when I have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, I frequently utter this inspired exclamation:
“Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna):
“For one in whose inner self there are no agitations...”
Thus he has transcended both existence and non-existence;
that one who is free from fear, happy, and sorrowless—
the gods do not even attain the sight of him.”
2. The Story of Devadatta.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Anupiyā for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Kosambī.
Wandering by stages on his tour, he eventually arrived at Kosambī.
There the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then, while Devadatta was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Whom now might I inspire with confidence, such that through his confidence great gain and honor would accrue to me?"
Then it occurred to Devadatta:
"This Prince Ajātasattu is both young and destined for greatness in the future.
What if I were to win the favor of Prince Ajātasattu?"
“With him being pleased with me, great gain and honor will arise for me.
Then Devadatta, having tidied his lodgings and taken his bowl and robe, set out for Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Rājagaha.
Then Devadatta, withdrawing his own form and manifesting the form of a young boy, appeared in the lap of Prince Ajātasattu, who was girded with a snake-girdle.
Then Prince Ajātasattu became afraid, agitated, apprehensive, and terrified.
Thereupon Devadatta said this to Prince Ajātasattu:
“Are you afraid of me, young man?
“Yes, I am afraid. “Who are you?”
“I am Devadatta.
“If you are indeed the venerable Devadatta, Bhante, then please appear in your own form.
Thereupon, Devadatta withdrew his appearance as a young boy and stood before Prince Ajātasattu, wearing his outer robe and carrying his bowl and robes.
Then Prince Ajātasattu, having gained deep confidence in Devadatta through this miracle of psychic power,
went to attend upon him morning and evening with five hundred chariots, and five hundred servings of rice-porridge were brought as a food offering.
Then, Devadatta, overcome by gain, honor, and fame, and with his mind completely possessed by them, a desire such as this arose:
“I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
With the mere arising of that thought, Devadatta’s psychic power vanished.
Now at that time, a son of the Koḷiyans named Kakudha, who had been the attendant of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having recently passed away, was reborn in a certain mind-made body.
His acquisition of such a physical form is like that of two or three Magadhan village-fields.
By means of that acquisition of a physical form, he harms neither himself nor others.
Then the young deva Kakudha approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deva Kakudha said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
"Bhante, Devadatta, being overwhelmed by gain, honor, and fame, and with his mind possessed by them, such a desire arose in him:..."
‘I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
With the mere arising of that thought, venerable sir, Devadatta fell away from that psychic power.
This is what the young deva Kakudha said.
Having said this, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, my attendant named Kakudha, the son of a Koḷiyān woman, has recently passed away and has been reborn in a certain mind-made body.
His acquisition of such a personal existence is like two or three Magadhan village-fields.”
Thus, by means of that acquisition of a personal existence, he harms neither himself nor others.
Then, venerable sir, the young deva Kakudha approached me; having approached, he paid homage to me and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, venerable sir, the young deva Kakudha said this to me:
“Venerable sir, when Devadatta’s mind was overwhelmed and possessed by gain, honor, and fame, such a desire arose in him:
‘I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Venerable sir, at the very moment that thought arose, Devadatta fell away from that psychic power.”
“This is what Kakudha, the son of the gods, said, bhante.
Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished right there.
“But Moggallāna, did you know with your own mind the mind of Kakudha, the son of the gods?”
“Whatever the young deva Kakudha says is exactly so and not otherwise?
“I have encompassed his mind with my own mind, venerable sir;
whatever the young deva Kakudha says is exactly so and not otherwise.”
“Guard this speech, Moggallāna! Guard this speech, Moggallāna!
Now that foolish man will reveal himself by his own doing.”
3. Discourse on the Five Teachers.
"Moggallāna, there are these five teachers found existing in the world.
Which five?"
“Here, Moggallāna, a certain teacher, being of impure virtue, claims: ‘I am of pure virtue; my virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.
Yet his disciples know him thus:
‘This venerable teacher, while being of impure virtue, claims: “I am of pure virtue; my virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.”’”
If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
And how could we conduct ourselves toward one whom that which is displeasing [to him] is unpleasant?
Furthermore, he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
‘Whatever he will do, by that alone he shall be known.
Moggallāna, it is such a teacher that his disciples protect in terms of virtue,
and such a teacher expects protection in terms of virtue from his disciples.
Furthermore, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, being one whose livelihood is impure, claims: "I am pure in livelihood; my livelihood is pure, bright, and undefiled.
His disciples know of him thus:
"This venerable teacher, while being one whose livelihood is impure, claims: 'I am pure in livelihood; my livelihood is pure, bright, and undefiled.'"
If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
And how could we behave toward one who finds something displeasing?
Furthermore, he is appointed with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
‘Whatever he does, by that alone shall he be known.
Moggallāna, such is the teacher whom his disciples protect in his livelihood,
and such is the teacher who expects protection in his livelihood from his disciples.”

Furthermore, Moggallāna, here some teacher, while his teaching of the Dhamma is impure, claims: "I am one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure; my teaching of the Dhamma is pure, radiant, and undefiled.
His disciples know him thus:
"This venerable teacher, while his teaching of the Dhamma is impure, claims: 'I am one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure,' and 'My teaching of the Dhamma is pure, radiant, and undefiled.'"
If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
And how could we conduct ourselves toward one whom this is displeasing?
Furthermore, he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
‘Whatever he will do, by that alone he will be known.
It is such a teacher, Moggallāna, that his disciples protect from the teaching of the Dhamma;
and such a teacher, moreover, expects protection from the teaching of the Dhamma from his disciples.
Furthermore, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, while his own exposition is impure, claims: "I am one whose exposition is pure; my exposition is pure, bright, and undefiled.
His disciples know of him thus:
"This venerable teacher, while his own exposition is impure, claims: 'I am one whose exposition is pure,' and 'My exposition is pure, bright, and undefiled.'"
If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
And how could we behave toward one who finds something displeasing?
Furthermore, he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
‘Whatever he will do, by that alone he will be known.
It is such a teacher, Moggallāna, that his disciples protect from being defined by his own words;
and such a teacher, moreover, expects protection from being defined by his words from his disciples.

Furthermore, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, being one whose knowledge and vision are impure, claims: "I am one whose knowledge and vision are pure; my knowledge and vision are pure, bright, and undefiled.
His disciples know of him thus:
"This venerable teacher, while being one whose knowledge and vision are impure, claims: 'I am one whose knowledge and vision are pure,' and 'My knowledge and vision are pure, bright, and undefiled.'"
If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
And how could we behave toward one who finds something displeasing?
Yet he is appointed with the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
‘Whatever he will do, by that alone he shall be known.
Moggallāna, disciples thus protect such a teacher from [the need for] knowledge and vision;
and such a teacher, in turn, expects protection from knowledge and vision from his disciples.
“Moggallāna, these five teachers are found existing in the world.
But as for me, Moggallāna, being one of pure virtue, I claim: ‘I am of pure virtue,’ and ‘My virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.
And my disciples do not guard me regarding my virtue.”
Nor do I expect protection by way of virtue from my disciples.
Being one whose livelihood is pure...
[and so on] ...being one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure... [and so on].
Being one whose exposition is completely pure...

[and so on] ...being one whose knowledge and vision is completely pure, I claim: "My knowledge and vision are completely pure," and "My knowledge and vision are completely pure, cleansed, and undefiled.
And my disciples do not protect me from [criticism regarding] my knowledge and vision.
"Nor do I expect protection from my disciples on account of their knowledge and vision.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kosambī for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Rājagaha.
There the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, Prince Ajātasattu goes to wait upon Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots,
and five hundred servings of food from the cooking-pots are brought as an offering.
“Monks, do not envy the gain, honor, and fame of Devadatta.”
"As long as, monks, Prince Ajātasattu goes to attend upon Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots,
and five hundred servings of cooked rice are brought as an offering of food,
only decline, monks, is to be expected for Devadatta regarding wholesome qualities, not growth."
“Just as if, monks, one were to break bile into the nose of a fierce dog, that dog would become even more fierce than before; even so, monks,
for as long as Prince Ajātasattu goes to attend upon Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots,
and five hundred servings of cooked rice are brought as an offering of food, [Devadatta will continue to decline].”
“Monks, only decline in wholesome qualities is to be expected for Devadatta, not growth.
Gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his own destruction; gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his ruin.
Just as, monks, the plantain tree bears fruit to its own destruction and bears fruit to its ruin;”
In the same way, monks, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his own destruction; gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his ruin.

Just as, monks, a bamboo bears fruit to its own destruction and bears fruit to its ruin, even so, monks, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his own destruction; gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his ruin.
“Just as, monks, the reed yields fruit for its own destruction and yields fruit for its ruin;
even so, monks, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction, and gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his ruin.
Just as, monks, a mule conceives for her own destruction and conceives for her ruin;”
In the same way, monks, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his own destruction; gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta to his ruin.
Indeed, the fruit destroys the plantain tree;
the fruit destroys the bamboo; the fruit destroys the reed.
"Honor kills the base man,
just as a fetus kills the mule.
The first recitation section is finished.
1. The Act of Proclamation.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was seated, surrounded by a large assembly including kings and their retinues, teaching the Dhamma.
Then Devadatta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One is now old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life.
Let the Blessed One now live free from anxiety, devoted to dwelling in happiness in this very life; let him hand over the community of monks to me.
I shall look after the community of monks.”
“Enough, Devadatta; let it not please you to lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
A second time, Devadatta...
[and] a third time, Devadatta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One is now old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life.
Let the Blessed One now live free from anxiety, devoted to dwelling in happiness in this very life; let him hand over the community of monks to me.
I shall look after the community of monks.”
“Devadatta, I would not entrust the Saṅgha of bhikkhus even to Sāriputta and Moggallāna; how much less to you, a wretch, a spittle-sucker!
Then Devadatta thought:
“The Blessed One has insulted me with the term ‘spittle-sucker’ before an assembly including the king, while praising Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”
Angry and displeased, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
This was the first instance of Devadatta’s resentment toward the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha perform a formal act of proclamation against Devadatta in Rājagaha:
‘Formerly Devadatta had one nature; now he has another nature.
Whatever Devadatta may do by body or speech, the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha is not to be seen therein; Devadatta alone is to be seen therein.’”
And furthermore, monks, it should be done in this way:
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha carry out a formal act of proclamation against Devadatta in Rājagaha:
“Formerly, Devadatta had one nature; now he has another.
Whatever Devadatta does by body or speech, because of that the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha is not to be regarded; rather, Devadatta himself is to be regarded for that.”
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs:
the Sangha is performing a formal act of proclamation against Devadatta in Rājagaha.
“Formerly Devadatta had one nature; now he has another nature.
Whatever Devadatta may do by way of body or speech, the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha is not to be seen therein; Devadatta alone is to be seen therein.
To whichever venerable one it is agreeable that the formal act of proclamation against Devadatta in Rājagaha be carried out—

“Formerly Devadatta had one nature, but now he has another nature. Whatever Devadatta may do by way of body or speech, the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha should not be regarded through that; rather, it is Devadatta himself who should be regarded through that.
He remained silent;
whoever did not approve should speak.
The Saṅgha has performed a formal act of disclosure against Devadatta in Rājagaha:
“Formerly Devadatta had one nature; now he has another nature.
Whatever Devadatta may do by body or speech, the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha is not to be regarded thereby; Devadatta alone is to be regarded thereby.”
“The Saṅgha approves; therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“In that case, Sāriputta, you must expose Devadatta in Rājagaha.”
“Venerable sir, previously I spoke in praise of Devadatta in Rājagaha, saying, ‘The son of Godhī is of great psychic power; the son of Godhī is of great majesty.
Venerable sir, how should I proclaim Devadatta in Rājagaha?”
“Did you not, Sāriputta, speak of Devadatta’s excellence in Rājagaha as being real, saying:
‘The son of Godhī has great psychic power; the son of Godhī has great majesty’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“In this very way, Sāriputta, you must reveal Devadatta’s true nature in Rājagaha.
“Yes, Bhante,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha authorize Sāriputta to proclaim Devadatta in Rājagaha:
‘Formerly Devadatta had one nature; now he has another nature.
Whatever Devadatta should do by body or speech, one should not regard that as the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; rather, one should regard it as Devadatta himself.’”
And furthermore, monks, he should be appointed in this way.
First, Sāriputta should be requested.
Having requested him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize the Venerable Sāriputta to proclaim Devadatta in Rājagaha:
‘Formerly Devadatta had one nature; now he has another nature.’”
"Whatever Devadatta should do by way of body or speech, by that neither the Buddha, nor the Dhamma, nor the Saṅgha is to be seen; rather, it is Devadatta alone who is to be seen by that.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
The Saṅgha appoints the Venerable Sāriputta to proclaim Devadatta in Rājagaha:

"Formerly, Devadatta had one nature; now he has another nature. Whatever Devadatta does by way of body or speech, the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha should not be regarded as being thereby affected; rather, Devadatta alone should be regarded as being affected by it.
To whichever Venerable it is pleasing, let him approve the appointment of the Venerable Sāriputta to proclaim Devadatta in Rājagaha.

“Formerly Devadatta had one nature, but now he has another nature. Whatever Devadatta does by way of body or speech, it should not be regarded as the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; it should be regarded as Devadatta himself.”—He who approves of this should remain silent;
he who does not approve should speak.
The Saṅgha has authorized the Venerable Sāriputta to proclaim Devadatta in Rājagaha:
“Formerly, Devadatta had one nature; now he has another nature.
Whatever Devadatta does by body or speech, one should not regard that as the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; rather, one should regard it as Devadatta himself.”
“The Saṅgha approves; therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this.
And the Venerable Sāriputta, having been authorized, entered Rājagaha together with a number of bhikkhus and made Devadatta known throughout Rājagaha:
“Formerly Devadatta’s nature was one thing; now his nature is another.”
“Whatever Devadatta might do by way of body or speech, one should not regard that as the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; rather, one should regard it as Devadatta himself.
In this regard, those people who were faithless, lacking confidence, and of poor understanding said:
“These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are envious; they are envious of Devadatta’s gain and honor.”
But those people who were faithful, confident, wise, competent, and intelligent said this:
"This will not be insignificant; it must be that the Blessed One is having Devadatta executed in Rājagaha.
2. The Story of Prince Ajātasattu.
Then Devadatta approached Prince Ajātasattu; having approached, he said this to Prince Ajātasattu:
"In the past, Prince, humans were long-lived; nowadays they are short-lived.
It is indeed possible that you, while still a prince, might pass away."
"In that case, prince, kill your father and become king;
I shall kill the Blessed One and become a Buddha.
Then Prince Ajātasattu—
“Venerable Devadatta is of great psychic power and great majesty; you should know, venerable sir, that it was Venerable Devadatta!
Having bound a tourniquet upon his thigh, terrified, agitated, apprehensive, and trembling, he suddenly entered the inner palace.
The high officials on guard at the inner palace saw Prince Ajātasattu entering the inner palace suddenly, terrified, agitated, apprehensive, and trembling.
Having seen him, they seized him.
While searching him, they saw a small pouch tied to his thigh and said this to Prince Ajātasattu:
"What do you intend to do, prince?"
“I desired to kill my father.
“By whom were you incited?
“By the noble Devadatta.”
Some high ministers formed this opinion:
“The prince must be killed, Devadatta must be killed, and all the monks must be killed.
Some other high ministers formed this opinion:
“Monks are not to be killed.
Monks have done nothing wrong.
It is the prince and Devadatta who must be killed.”
Some high officials formed this opinion:
"Neither the prince nor Devadatta should be killed;
nor should the monks be killed."
"It should be reported to the king.
We shall do exactly as the king says.
Then those high ministers, taking Prince Ajātasattu with them, went to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha; having arrived, they reported this matter to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
“How, my good man, was the counsel decided upon by the high ministers?
“Some of the high ministers, Your Majesty, gave this counsel:
‘The prince must be killed, Devadatta must be killed, and all the monks must be killed.’”
Some high officials formed this opinion:
“The monks must not be killed.
The monks have committed no offense.”
‘The prince must be killed, and Devadatta as well.
But some high ministers formed this opinion:
‘Neither the prince nor Devadatta should be killed.’
“The monks must not be killed.
We should inform the king;
we will do exactly as the king says.”
“What, I say, can the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha do?
Has the Blessed One not already made Devadatta notorious in Rājagaha beforehand, saying:
‘Formerly Devadatta had one nature; now his nature is different’?”
“Whatever Devadatta might do by way of body or speech, one should not regard that as the Buddha, nor the Dhamma, nor the Saṅgha; rather, one should regard it as Devadatta himself.
In this matter, those high officials who formed the opinion:
“The prince must be killed, and Devadatta as well;”
"And all the monks must be killed"— he did this at an improper time and in an unseemly manner.
Those high officials who had formed such an opinion...
“Monks are not to be killed;
monks have done nothing wrong;
rather, it is the prince and Devadatta who must be killed.”
He placed them in low positions.
As for those high ministers who had thought thus:
"Neither the prince nor Devadatta should be killed..."
“Monks must not be killed;
it should be reported to the king;
we shall do whatever the king says.”
He placed him in a high position.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to Prince Ajātasattu:
"Why do you wish to kill me, prince?"
“I am in need of the kingdom, Your Majesty,” he said.
“If you, prince, are indeed in need of the kingdom, here is your kingdom,” he replied, and he handed over the kingdom to Prince Ajātasattu.
3. The Sending of the Assassins.
Then Devadatta went to Prince Ajātasattu and, having approached him, said this to Prince Ajātasattu:
"Great King, give orders to men who will deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.
Then Prince Ajātasattu gave orders to his men.
“Friend, you should do exactly as the noble Devadatta says.
Then Devadatta commanded a man:
“Go, friend, the ascetic Gotama is staying in such-and-such a place.”
“Having deprived him of life, come back by this path,” he said.
He stationed two men on that path,
saying, “Whichever single man comes along this path, deprive him of life and return by this path.”
On that road he stationed four men, saying:
"When two men come along this road, you must deprive them of life and then proceed along this same road.
On that road he stationed eight men.
“Kill those four men who come by this path and then proceed along it.
He stationed sixteen men on that path, saying:
“Kill those eight men who come by this path and then proceed.”
Then that man, taking up his sword and shield and buckling on his bow and quiver, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he stood not far from the Blessed One, frightened, agitated, suspicious, and terrified, with his body rigid.
The Blessed One saw that man standing there, frightened, agitated, suspicious, and terrified, with his body rigid.
Having seen him, he said this to that man:
"Come, friend; do not be afraid.

Then that man, having placed his sword and shield to one side and set aside his bow and quiver, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me—foolish as I was, deluded as I was, and unwholesome as I was—in that I approached here with a mind of ill will and a murderous intent.
Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.
“Surely, friend, a transgression has overcome you—foolish as you were, deluded as you were, and unwholesome as you were—in that you approached here with a mind of ill will and a murderous intent.”
"But since you, friend, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.
For this, friend, is growth in the discipline of the Noble Ones:
that one who sees a transgression as a transgression makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future."
Then the Blessed One gave that man a graduated discourse, namely:
a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that his mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, then he revealed that teaching of the Dhamma which is uniquely proclaimed by the Buddhas.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up the dye, even so, while that man was on that very seat, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose: [that all which is subject to arising is subject to cessation].
“Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.

Then that man, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma; having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence, and no longer dependent on others in the Teacher’s instruction, said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!”

"Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One through many lines of reasoning."
“Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
Then the Blessed One said this to that man:
"Do not go by this path, friend; go by that path," he said, directing him along another route.
Then those two men thought, "Why indeed does that one man take so long to return?"
As they were traveling along the road, they saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
Having seen him, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
To them, the Blessed One delivered a gradual discourse... [and so forth].
Independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, they said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante!
… [as before] … May the Blessed One accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
Then the Blessed One said this to those men:
“Friends, do not go by this path; go by this other path,” and he sent them away by another route.
Then those four men... [as before]...
Then those eight men...
[and so on] ...then those sixteen men thought:
"Why indeed are those eight men taking so long to return?"
As they were traveling along the road, they saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
Having seen him, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
To them, the Blessed One delivered a graduated discourse, that is to say:
Having given a discourse on giving … [and so forth] … being independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instruction, they said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! … [and so forth] …”
“May the Blessed One accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.
Then the Blessed One said to those men, “Friends, do not go by this road; go by this other road,” and he sent them off by another path.
Then that man approached Devadatta; having approached him, he said this to Devadatta:
"Venerable sir, I am not able to deprive the Blessed One of life;
the Blessed One is of great psychic power and great majesty."
“Enough, friend;
do not deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.
I myself shall deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.”
4. The Act of Shedding Blood.
At that time, the Blessed One was walking back and forth in the shade of Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then Devadatta, having climbed Vulture Peak Mountain, hurled down a large rock.
"By this means, I shall deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.
Two mountain peaks met together and caught that rock.
Then, as she leaped up, she struck the Blessed One's feet and drew blood.
Then the Blessed One, looking upward, said this to Devadatta:
"Much demerit has been produced by you, foolish man, in that with a wicked mind and a murderous intent, you drew blood from the Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, this was the first deed of immediate retribution accumulated by Devadatta, namely, that with a wicked mind and a murderous intent he drew blood from the Tathāgata.
The bhikkhus heard:
“It seems Devadatta has plotted the murder of the Blessed One.”

Those monks were walking back and forth all around the Blessed One’s dwelling, reciting their lessons with loud voices and great noise for the sake of guarding, protecting, and defending the Blessed One.
The Blessed One heard that loud voice, that great noise, that sound of recitation.
Having heard it, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, what is this loud noise, this great clamor, this sound of recitation?
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhus heard it was said:
‘Devadatta has indeed plotted the murder of the Blessed One.’”

“Venerable sir, those bhikkhus are walking back and forth all around the Blessed One’s dwelling, reciting their lessons with loud voices and great noise for the sake of the Blessed One’s protection, defense, and security.
This, venerable sir, is that loud voice, that great noise, the sound of recitation.
“In that case, Ānanda, address those bhikkhus in my name:”
“The Teacher summons the Venerables.
“Yes, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and he approached those bhikkhus. Having approached, he said this to those bhikkhus:
“The Teacher summons the Venerables.”
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. They approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to them:
“Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life by means of an external assault.”
“Monks, Tathāgatas attain final nibbāna without exertion.
Monks, there are these five teachers found existing in the world.
Which five?”
In this case, monks, a certain teacher, being of impure virtue, claims: "I am pure in virtue," and "My virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.
His disciples know him thus:
"This venerable teacher, while being of impure virtue, claims: 'I am pure in virtue,' and 'My virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.'"
If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
And how could we behave toward one who finds something displeasing?
Furthermore, he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
‘Whatever he will do, by that alone he will be known.
It is such a teacher, monks, that his disciples protect in terms of virtue;
and such a teacher, in turn, expects protection in terms of virtue from his disciples.
Furthermore, monks, here some teacher, being one whose livelihood is impure …pe… being one whose teaching of the Dhamma is impure …pe… being one whose exposition is impure …pe…
Being one whose knowledge and vision are impure, he claims: "I am one whose knowledge and vision are pure," and "My knowledge and vision are pure, cleansed, and undefiled.
His disciples know of him thus:
"This venerable teacher, being one whose knowledge and vision are impure, claims: 'I am one whose knowledge and vision are pure,' and 'My knowledge and vision are pure, cleansed, and undefiled.'"
"If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
And how could we behave toward one who is displeased with us?
Yet he is appointed [to receive] robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
‘Whatever he will do, by that alone he shall be known.
In such a way, monks, disciples protect a teacher from [the charge of] lack of knowledge and vision;
and such a teacher, in turn, expects protection from lack of knowledge and vision from his disciples.
“Monks, these five teachers are found existing in the world.
But as for me, monks, being of pure virtue, I claim: ‘I am of pure virtue,’ and ‘My virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.
And my disciples do not have to protect me regarding my virtue.”
And I do not expect protection in terms of virtue from my disciples.
For I, monks, being one whose livelihood is pure...
[and] being one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure... [and so forth].
Being one whose analytical exposition is completely pure...

[and so on] ...being one whose knowledge and vision is completely pure, I claim: "I am one whose knowledge and vision is completely pure," and "My knowledge and vision is completely pure, bright, and undefiled.
Furthermore, my disciples do not need to protect me regarding my knowledge and vision.
Nor do I expect protection for my knowledge and vision from my disciples.
"It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life by means of an external assault.
Monks, Tathāgatas attain final Nibbāna without such an assault."
“Go, monks, each to your respective dwellings.
Monks, the Tathāgatas do not need protection. 5.
The Sending of Nāḷāgiri.
Now at that time, there was an elephant in Rājagaha named Nāḷāgiri who was fierce and a killer of men.
Then Devadatta, having entered Rājagaha, went to the elephant stable and said this to the elephant keepers:
“Friends, we are indeed known as the King’s kinsmen; we are capable of placing those in low positions in high positions, and we can increase their food and wages.”
"In that case, my good man, when the ascetic Gotama has entered this street, release the elephant Nāḷāgiri and lead him into this street.
"Very well, venerable sir," those elephant trainers replied to Devadatta.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms together with a large company of bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One entered that street.
Those elephant trainers saw the Blessed One entering that street;
having seen him, they released the elephant Nāḷāgiri and drove it into that street.
The elephant Nāḷāgiri saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, he raised his trunk, with his ears and tail erect, and rushed toward where the Blessed One was.
Those monks also saw the elephant Nāḷāgiri coming from afar.
Having seen him, they said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this elephant Nāḷāgiri, fierce and a killer of men, has entered this street.
Let the Blessed One step back, venerable sir."
“Let the Sugata depart. “Come, monks; do not be afraid.
It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life by means of an external assault.”
“Bhikkhus, Tathāgatas attain final nibbāna without exertion.
A second time those bhikkhus...
[and] a third time those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this elephant Nāḷāgiri is fierce and a slayer of men; he has entered this street.
Let the Blessed One step back, venerable sir;
let the Sugata step back.”
“Come, bhikkhus, do not be afraid.
It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that anyone should deprive a Tathāgata of life by means of an external assault.
Tathāgatas, bhikkhus, attain final Nibbāna without such an assault.”
Now at that time, people were staying on terraces, on balconies, and under awnings.
There, those people who were faithless, lacking confidence, and dull-witted said this:
"How handsome indeed is that great ascetic! He will surely be harassed by the nāga."
But those people who were faithful, confident, wise, competent, and intelligent said this:
"Ah, sirs, before long the elephant will surely encounter the elephant!
Then the Blessed One suffused the elephant Nālāgiri with a mind of loving-kindness.
Then the elephant Nāḷāgiri, touched by the Blessed One’s mind of loving-kindness, lowered his trunk and approached the Blessed One; having approached, he stood before the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, stroking the forehead of the elephant Nāḷāgiri with his right hand, addressed the elephant Nāḷāgiri with these verses:
"Do not, O elephant, attack the Naga!"
For it is suffering, O elephant, to attack a noble one;
for one struck by a noble one, O elephant,
there is no happy rebirth hereafter.
Let there be neither intoxication nor negligence,
for those who are negligent do not go to a happy destination;
you alone shall act accordingly.
"By which you shall go to a happy destination.

Then the elephant Nāḷāgiri, taking the dust from the Blessed One’s feet with his trunk and scattering it over his own head, backed away while still looking back at the Blessed One until he reached the elephant stable.
There, the elephant Nāḷāgiri went to the elephant stable and stood in his own place.
And likewise, Nāḷāgiri the elephant was tamed.
At that time, people were singing this verse:
“Some tame with the rod;”
With goads and with whips;
by the Great Seer, the elephant was tamed without rod and without sword.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying, “How wicked is this Devadatta, how unfortunate!
For he would even strive for the death of the ascetic Gotama, who possesses such great psychic power and such great majesty.
Thus, Devadatta’s gain and honor declined.
And the gains and honors of the Blessed One increased.
At that time, Devadatta, having lost his gains and honors, ate by repeatedly making requests from families along with his retinue.
People criticized, complained, and grumbled:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, eat by repeatedly making requests among families?
To whom would what is well-prepared not be pleasing? To whom would what is delicious not be agreeable?”
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
"How can Devadatta, together with his retinue, eat after repeatedly soliciting from families?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
"Is it true, Devadatta, that you and your followers eat by repeatedly making requests from families?
"It is true, Blessed One."... [as before] ...
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Therefore, monks, I shall prescribe for the monks the practice of eating in groups of three among families, based on three reasons for its benefit.”
For the restraint of individuals who are difficult to correct;
for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus; so that those with evil desires, by resorting to a faction, might not cause a schism in the Saṅgha;
and out of compassion for the families.
“In the case of eating in a group, the rule of the Dhamma must be applied.
Then Devadatta approached Kokālika, Kaṭamodakatissaka, Khaṇḍadeviyā-putta, and Samuddadatta;
having approached them, he said this to Kokālika, Kaṭamodakatissaka, Khaṇḍadeviyā-putta, and Samuddadatta:
“Come, friends, let us cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama, a schism in the Wheel.
When this was said, Kokālika said this to Devadatta:
“The ascetic Gotama, friend, is of great psychic power and great majesty.”
"How might we cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama, a schism in the Wheel?
"Come, friends, let us approach the ascetic Gotama and request five points:

'Venerable sir, in many ways the Blessed One speaks in praise of fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, ascetic practices, inspiring confidence, reduction of burdens, and the arousal of energy.'"
“Venerable sir, these five bases lead in many ways to fewness of wishes, to contentment, to effacement, to the ascetic practices, to agreeableness, to non-involvement, to the arousal of energy.
It would be good, venerable sir, if monks were forest-dwellers for life; whoever should enter a village area, let a fault touch him.
May they be almsfood-eaters for life; whoever should accept an invitation, let a fault touch him.”
‘For as long as life lasts, they should be rag-robe wearers; whoever should accept a robe from a householder, let him incur a fault.
For as long as life lasts, they should be tree-root dwellers; whoever should resort to a roofed dwelling, let him incur a fault.
For as long as life lasts, they should not eat fish or meat; whoever should eat fish or meat, let him incur a fault.’”
“The ascetic Gotama will not permit these five points.
We shall convince the people by means of these five points.
“It is indeed possible, friends, to cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama, a breaking of the wheel, by means of these five points.”
“For people, friends, have confidence in what is coarse.
Then Devadatta, together with his retinue, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, Devadatta said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, the Blessed One has in many ways praised fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, asceticism, serenity, reduction [of defilements], and the arousal of energy.
Bhante, these five things lead in many ways to fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, asceticism, serenity, reduction, and the arousal of energy.
It would be good, Bhante, if the bhikkhus were forest-dwellers for as long as life lasts; whoever should enter a village area, let a fault touch him.”
"For as long as life lasts, they should be almsfood eaters; whoever should accept an invitation, let a fault touch him.
For as long as life lasts, they should be rag-robe wearers; whoever should accept a robe from a householder, let a fault touch him.
For as long as life lasts, they should be tree-root dwellers; whoever should resort to a roofed dwelling, let a fault touch him."
“For as long as life lasts, they should not eat fish or meat; whoever eats fish or meat would incur blame.
“Enough, Devadatta!
Let whoever wishes be a forest-dweller; let whoever wishes dwell near a village.”
"Whoever wishes, let him be an alms-food eater; whoever wishes, let him accept invitations.
Whoever wishes, let him be a wearer of rag-robes; whoever wishes, let him accept robes from householders.
For eight months, Devadatta, I have authorized the lodging at the foot of a tree."
“Fish and meat that are pure in three respects—
unseen, unheard, and unsuspected. Then Devadatta—
“The Blessed One does not authorize these five points”—
thus, joyful and elated, he rose from his seat together with his followers, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with his right side toward him,
and departed. Then Devadatta, together with his followers, entered Rājagaha and persuaded the people by means of those five points.
“Friends, we approached the ascetic Gotama and requested five points:
‘Venerable sir, in many ways the Blessed One speaks in praise of one who has few desires … [and so on] … of one who exerts energy.’”
“Venerable sir, these five grounds lead in many ways to fewness of desires … [and so on] … to the arousal of energy.
It would be good, venerable sir, if the bhikkhus were forest-dwellers for as long as life lasts; whoever should enter a village area, let a fault touch him … [and so on].”
"For as long as life lasts, they should not eat fish or meat; whoever should eat fish or meat, let blame touch him.
The ascetic Gotama does not permit these five things.
We, having undertaken these five things, live accordingly."
In that regard, those people who were faithless, lacking confidence, and of poor understanding said this:
“These ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, are indeed austere and live a life of effacement;
but the ascetic Gotama is luxurious and intends for luxury.”
But those people who were faithful, confident, wise, competent, and intelligent, complained, grumbled, and protested:
"How can Devadatta indeed strive for a schism in the Blessed One's Saṅgha, for a breaking of the Wheel?
The bhikkhus heard those people complaining, grumbling, and protesting.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can Devadatta indeed strive for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a breaking of the Wheel?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so forth].
“Is it true, Devadatta, that you are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a schism in the Wheel?
“It is true, Blessed One.
“Enough, Devadatta.”
Do not let schism in the Saṅgha be pleasing to you.
Schism in the Saṅgha, Devadatta, is a grave matter.
Whoever, Devadatta, causes a harmonious Saṅgha to split, produces an evil deed that lasts for an eon; he will boil in hell for an eon.
But whoever, Devadatta, reunites a split Saṅgha, generates sublime merit and rejoices in heaven for an eon.
Enough, Devadatta!
Let not schism in the Saṅgha be pleasing to you.
“Devadatta, a schism in the Saṅgha is indeed grave.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
Devadatta saw the Venerable Ānanda walking for alms in Rājagaha.
Having seen him, he approached the Venerable Ānanda and, having approached, said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"From this day forward, friend Ānanda, apart from the Blessed One and apart from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, I shall perform the Uposatha and carry out the formal acts of the Saṅgha.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from his almsround after his meal, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this morning, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Rājagaha for alms.
While I was walking for alms in Rājagaha, Venerable sir, Devadatta saw me."
Having seen me, he approached me; having approached, he said this to me:
“From this day forward, friend Ānanda, apart from the Blessed One and apart from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, I shall perform the Uposatha and I shall carry out the formal acts of the Saṅgha.
“Venerable sir, from this day forward Devadatta will split the Saṅgha.”
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:
“Good is easily done by the good;
Good is difficult for the evil to do.”
“Evil is easily done by the evil,
but evil is difficult for the noble ones to do.
The second recitation section is finished.
1. The Discourse on the Schism in the Saṅgha.
Then, on that very Uposatha day, Devadatta rose from his seat and took a voting ticket, saying:
"Friends, we approached the ascetic Gotama and requested five points."
“Bhante, the Blessed One has in many ways spoken in praise of one who has few desires … [and so on] … of one who exerts energy.
Bhante, these five things have in many ways been spoken of for the sake of having few desires … [and so on] …”
“They lead to the arousal of energy.
It would be good, Bhante, if the bhikkhus were forest-dwellers for as long as life lasts;
whoever should enter a village area, let a fault touch him… [as before] … they should not eat fish or meat for as long as life lasts; whoever should eat fish or meat, let a fault touch him.”
“The ascetic Gotama does not allow these five points.
We shall adopt and practice these five points.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of these five points, let him take a voting ticket.”
Now at that time, about five hundred Vajjiputta monks from Vesālī were newly ordained and ignorant of the Dhamma.
They took voting tickets, thinking, “This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya; this is the Teacher’s instruction.
Then Devadatta, having split the Saṅgha, departed for Gayāsīsa taking those five hundred monks with him.
Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, Devadatta has split the Saṅgha and, taking about five hundred bhikkhus with him, has set out for Gayāsīsa.”
“Sāriputta, do you truly have no compassion for those young bhikkhus?
Go, Sāriputta, before those bhikkhus meet with calamity and disaster.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Sāriputta and Moggallāna replied to the Blessed One. They rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to their right, they went to Gayāsīsa.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was standing not far from the Blessed One, weeping.
Then the Blessed One said this to that bhikkhu:
"Bhikkhu, why are you weeping?"
“Venerable sir, even those who are the Blessed One’s chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, go into the presence of Devadatta, finding pleasure in his teaching.
“This is impossible, monk, it cannot happen, that Sāriputta and Moggallāna would find pleasure in Devadatta’s teaching. However, they went there for the sake of reconciling the monks.
Now at that time, Devadatta was sitting surrounded by a large assembly, teaching the Dhamma.
Devadatta saw Sāriputta and Moggallāna coming from afar.
Having seen them, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Behold, bhikkhus, how well-expounded is the Dhamma by me! Even those who were the foremost disciples of the ascetic Gotama, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, are now coming into my presence.”
“May they find delight in my Dhamma.
When this was said, Kokālika spoke thus to Devadatta:
“Friend Devadatta, do not place your trust in Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”
“Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.
“Enough, friend.
Welcome to them, since they find pleasure in my Dhamma.”
Then Devadatta invited the Venerable Sāriputta to share half his seat,
saying, "Come, friend Sāriputta, sit here. "Enough,
friend," the Venerable Sāriputta replied, and taking another seat, he sat down to one side.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also took a certain seat and sat down to one side.
Then Devadatta, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dharma for much of the night, requested the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is free from sloth and torpor."
“Let it occur to you, friend Sāriputta, to give a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus; my back aches, so I shall stretch it.
“Very well, friend,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to Devadatta.
Then Devadatta spread out his outer robe folded fourfold and lay down on his right side.
As he was weary, with mindfulness lost and lacking clear comprehension, sleep fell upon him for a moment.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta exhorted and instructed the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk by means of the instruction of the miracle of mind-reading.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna exhorted and instructed the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk by means of the instruction of the miracle of psychic power.

Then, as those bhikkhus were being exhorted and instructed by the Venerable Sāriputta through the miracle of direct address and by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna through the miracle of psychic power, the dustless,
stainless Eye of Dhamma arose in them.
“Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One.”
"Whoever approves of that Blessed One’s Dhamma, let him come.
Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna, taking those five hundred bhikkhus, went to the Bamboo Grove.
Thereupon Kokālika roused Devadatta from his seat.
“Arise, friend Devadatta! Your monks have been led away by Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Did I not say to you, friend Devadatta:
‘Friend Devadatta, do not place your trust in Sāriputta and Moggallāna’?”
“Are Sāriputta and Moggallāna of evil desires, having fallen under the sway of evil desires?
At that very moment, hot blood gushed from Devadatta’s mouth.
Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be good, Bhante, if monks who follow those who cause schism could be ordained again.
“Enough, Sāriputta.”
"Do not approve of the re-ordination of those monks who follow the schismatics.
Therefore, Sāriputta, have those monks who follow the schismatics confess a grave offense (thullaccaya).
But how, Sāriputta, did Devadatta conduct himself?"
“Venerable sir, just as the Blessed One has spent much of the night instructing, urging, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk, he then requests me:
‘Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is free from sloth and torpor;
let a Dhamma talk occur to you, Sāriputta, for the bhikkhus. My back aches, so I shall stretch it.’”
“In the same way, Bhante, Devadatta proceeded.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“In the past, bhikkhus, there was a great lake in a forest wilderness.”
The elephants lived depending on that lake.
Having plunged into that lake, they pulled up lotus roots and stalks with their trunks; having rinsed them thoroughly, they chewed them free of mud and swallowed them.
This served both for their beauty and for their strength.
And on that account, they do not meet death or suffering amounting to death.

But, monks, those young elephant calves who are training after the example of those great elephants, having plunged into that lake and pulled up lotus roots with their trunks, do not rinse them well; instead, they chew them while still covered in mud and swallow them.
That [practice] leads neither to their beauty nor to their strength;
on that account, they meet with death or with suffering amounting to death.
Even so, monks, Devadatta, out of compassion for me, will die a miserable death.
Like a bee that has devoured the mud, [I have emerged] from the Great Boar who was tossing up the earth, eating lotus roots, and roaming by the rivers.
"Thinking, 'May he not die in misery, having no one to show him compassion,' [he goes].
Monks, a monk endowed with eight qualities is worthy to go on a mission.
With which eight? "What eight?"

“Here, monks, a monk is a listener, a speaker, one who has learned, one who retains, one who understands, one who makes others understand, skilled in what is relevant and irrelevant, and not a maker of quarrels—
it is endowed with these eight qualities, monks, that a monk is worthy to go on an errand.
Endowed with these eight qualities, monks, Sāriputta is worthy to go on an errand.”

"By which eight? Here, monks, Sāriputta is a listener, a proclaimer, a receiver, a retainer, one who understands, one who makes others understand, skilled in what is relevant and irrelevant, and not a maker of quarrels—
it is by possessing these eight qualities, monks, that Sāriputta is worthy to go on a mission."
He who, having entered an assembly of fierce speech,
does not tremble and does not falter in his words—
Nor does he conceal the teaching;
he explains it without hesitation,
and when questioned, he is not provoked to anger.
"Indeed, such a bhikkhu is worthy of going on an errand.
"Monks, Devadatta, overcome and possessed by eight things that are not the true Dhamma, is destined for the plane of misery, destined for hell, staying there for an eon, incurable."
"By what eight?
Devadatta, monks, being overcome and his mind consumed by gain, is destined for a state of misery, for hell, remaining there for an eon, beyond remedy.
By loss, monks... [and so on for the remaining seven]."
By gain, monks, ... by loss, monks, ...
by honor, monks, ... [and so forth].
"Monks, Devadatta—overcome and possessed by a mind of disrespect, monks... by evil desires, monks...
and by evil friendship, monks—is destined for the state of loss, destined for hell, remaining there for an eon, and beyond remedy."
"Monks, Devadatta, overcome and possessed by these eight unrighteous qualities, is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, beyond help.
It is good, monks, that a monk should dwell having repeatedly overcome gain when it arises; ... [and] loss when it arises;
... fame when it arises..."
... arisen ill repute ...
arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...
He should dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen evil desires... having repeatedly overcome arisen evil friends.
And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen gain for some purpose, and arisen loss...?
Renown that has arisen… ill-repute that has arisen… honor that has arisen…
Could one dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen lack of honor, arisen evil desires, and arisen evil friendship?

For whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise in one who dwells without having overcome acquired gain, monks—those taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist for one who dwells having repeatedly overcome acquired gain.
Whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise in one who dwells without having overcome non-acquisition... [and so on].
... arisen fame ...
arisen ill-repute ...
arisen honor ...

For one who dwells without having overcome disrespect that has arisen… evil desires that have arisen… evil friendship that has arisen, taints, vexations, and fevers may arise; but for one who dwells having repeatedly overcome evil friendship that has arisen, such taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist.
"It is for this purpose, monks, that one should dwell having repeatedly overcome whatever gain has arisen, whatever loss has arisen...
whatever fame has arisen,
whatever disrepute has arisen..."
... arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...
arisen evil desire ...
One should dwell having repeatedly overcome any arisen association with evil friends.
Therefore, monks, we shall dwell having repeatedly overcome any arisen gain, any arisen loss, ...
[and] any arisen fame...
... arisen ill repute ...
arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...
"Thinking, 'We shall dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen evil desires... having repeatedly overcome arisen evil friendship,' in this way,
monks, you should train yourselves."
“Bhikkhus, Devadatta, overcome and possessed by three things that are not true Dhamma, is destined for the plane of misery, for hell, to remain there for an eon, and is beyond help.
What are the three?
Evil desire, evil friendship, and he reached a state of complacency midway because of a mere trifling attainment of distinction.”
"Monks, Devadatta, being overcome by these three things that are not the true Dharma and with his mind consumed by them, is destined for the state of loss, for hell, remaining there for an eon,
incurable. May no one in this world ever arise with evil desires."
Therefore, you too should know the destination of those with evil desires;
even one renowned as "wise," [if he follows them...]
"He is considered one who has cultivated his own self;
he stands with glory like water—
thus have I heard regarding Devadatta."
Thus, having practiced negligence and having assailed the Tathāgata,
he fell into the Avīci hell.
It has four gates and is terrifying.
For he who would deceive one who is free from malice and does no evil deed—
That very evil touches him who is ill-intentioned and disrespectful,
as if pouring a jar of poison into the ocean.
Whoever might think to pollute it,
he cannot defile it by that means,
for the great ocean is formidable.
In the same way, whoever harms the Tathāgata—
who is in harmony and whose mind is peaceful— by means of debate;
In such a person, contentious speech does not take root.
A wise person should make such a one their friend and should associate with them.
“The bhikkhu who follows that path shall reach the destruction of suffering.
2. Upāli’s Questions.
Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“‘Schism in the Saṅgha, schism in the Saṅgha,’ it is said, Bhante.”
“To what extent, venerable sir, is there a schism in the Saṅgha that does not amount to a formal split of the Saṅgha?
And to what extent is there both a schism in the Saṅgha and a formal split of the Saṅgha?

“Upāli, when one person is on one side and two persons are on the other side, and a fourth person proclaims the motion and distributes voting tickets—this is a schism in the Saṅgha that does not amount to a formal split of the Saṅgha.”
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
In this way too, Upāli, there is a schism in the Saṅgha, but not a formal split of the Saṅgha.
When there are two on one side, Upāli, and two on the other, and a fifth proclaims the proclamation and distributes voting tickets—this is a mere dispute within the Saṅgha.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve of this.
In this way too, Upāli, there is a schism in the Saṅgha, but it is not a formal split of the Saṅgha.
When there are two on one side and three on the other, and the sixth proclaims [the motion] and distributes the voting tickets—this is a schism in the Saṅgha, but not a formal split of the Saṅgha.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve of this.
In this way too, Upāli, there is a schism in the Saṅgha, but not a formal split of the Saṅgha.
When there are three on one side and three on the other, and a seventh proclaims the motion and distributes the voting tickets—Upāli, [in this case] it is a mere quarrel.”
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve of this.
In this way too, Upāli, there is a schism in the Saṅgha, but it is not a formal split of the Saṅgha.

When there are three on one side and four on the other, and the eighth person proclaims the motion and distributes the voting tickets—this is a schism in the Saṅgha, but not a formal split of the Saṅgha.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve of this.
In this way too, Upāli, there is a schism in the Saṅgha, but it is not a formal split of the Saṅgha.
When there are four on one side and four on the other, and a ninth person proclaims the motion and distributes the voting tickets—this is a schism in the Saṅgha, but not a formal split of the Saṅgha.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
In this way, Upāli, there is both a schism in the Saṅgha and a formal split of the Saṅgha.
Or, Upāli, with nine or more than nine [monks], there is both a schism in the Saṅgha and a formal split of the Saṅgha.
“Upāli, it is not a bhikkhunī who splits the Saṅgha, though she may strive for its division;

nor does a female trainee split the Saṅgha …pe… nor does a male novice split the Saṅgha, nor a female novice, nor a male lay follower, nor a female lay follower, though they may strive for its division.
It is a regular bhikkhu, Upāli—one who belongs to the same community and stands within the same boundary—who splits the Saṅgha.”
“‘Schism in the Saṅgha, schism in the Saṅgha,’ it is said, Bhante.
To what extent, Bhante, is the Saṅgha considered split?
“In this case, Upāli, monks proclaim what is not Dhamma as Dhamma.”
They proclaim what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma.
They proclaim what is not discipline as discipline.
They proclaim what is discipline as not discipline.
They proclaim that what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim that what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim that what was not practiced by the Tathāgata was practiced by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as laid down by the Tathāgata;
and they proclaim what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not laid down by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what is not an offense as an offense;
they proclaim what is an offense as not an offense;
they proclaim a light offense as a grave offense.
They represent a grave offense as a light offense;
they represent an offense with remainder as an offense without remainder;
and they represent an offense without remainder as an offense with remainder.
They proclaim a grave offense as a non-grave offense;
they proclaim a non-grave offense as a grave offense.

By means of these eighteen grounds, they separate themselves, they separate themselves further, they perform the Uposatha separately, they perform the Pavāraṇā separately, and they carry out Saṅgha transactions separately.
"To this extent, Upāli, the Saṅgha is split.
"Venerable sir, it is said, 'concord of the Saṅgha, concord of the Saṅgha.
To what extent, venerable sir, is the Saṅgha in concord?"
“Here, Upāli, monks proclaim what is non-Dhamma as ‘non-Dhamma.
They proclaim what is Dhamma as ‘Dhamma.
They proclaim what is non-discipline as ‘non-discipline.’”
They proclaim what is discipline as "discipline.
They proclaim what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as "not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as "spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata."
