They proclaim what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what was practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as "not prescribed by the Tathāgata."
They proclaim what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as "prescribed by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what is not an offense as "not an offense," and they proclaim what is an offense as "an offense."
They proclaim a light offense as a light offense;
they proclaim a grave offense as a grave offense;
they proclaim an offense with remainder as an offense with remainder.
They explain a non-residual offense as a "non-residual offense.
They explain a grave offense as a "grave offense.
They explain a non-grave offense as a "non-grave offense."

“Because of these eighteen grounds, they do not separate themselves, they do not withdraw, they do not perform the Uposatha separately, they do not perform the Pavāraṇā separately, and they do not carry out Saṅgha business separately.
To this extent, Upāli, the Saṅgha is harmonious.
“But venerable sir, having split a harmonious Saṅgha, what does one produce?”
“Having split a united Saṅgha, Upāli, one generates an evil deed that lasts for an eon; one roasts in hell for an eon.
One who splits the Saṅgha is bound for the state of deprivation, bound for hell, staying there for an eon.”
Delighting in factions and established in unrighteousness,
one falls away from security from bondage;
having split a harmonious Saṅgha, [one suffers].
“He is cooked in hell for an eon.
“But, Bhante, having reunited a split Saṅgha, what does he produce?
“Upāli, having reunited a split Saṅgha, one produces sublime merit; one rejoices in heaven for an eon.”
Happy is concord in the Saṅgha,
and the assistance rendered to those in concord; one who delights in concord, established in the Dhamma, [is happy].
He does not fall away from the security of yoga;
having made the Saṅgha harmonious,
he rejoices in heaven for an eon.
“Could it be, Bhante, that one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is destined for the states of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an eon, and incurable?
“It could be, Upāli, that one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is destined for the states of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an eon, and incurable.
“But could it also be, Bhante, that one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is not destined for the states of deprivation, not destined for hell, not remaining there for an eon, and not incurable?”
“It may be, Upāli, that a schismatic of the Saṅgha is not one bound for the states of deprivation, not one bound for hell, not one destined to remain there for an eon, and not one incurable.
“But which kind of schismatic of the Saṅgha, venerable sir, is one bound for the states of deprivation, bound for hell, destined to remain there for an eon, and incurable?
“In this case, Upāli, a bhikkhu proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma.”

In that case, one who holds a view contrary to the Dhamma regarding a schism—misrepresenting the view, misrepresenting the approval, misrepresenting the preference, and misrepresenting the disposition—and proclaims it, distributing voting tickets, saying:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction;
accept this, approve of this”—such a person, Upāli, is a schismatic of the Saṅgha, destined for the states of deprivation, bound for hell, remaining there for an eon, and incurable.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma.

Having a view regarding that which is non-Dhamma, yet a view regarding the schism as being Dhamma, he sets aside his own view, sets aside his approval, sets aside his preference, and sets aside his disposition; he makes a proclamation and distributes voting tickets, saying:
"This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction. Accept this, approve of this."
This too, Upāli, is a schismatic who is bound for states of deprivation, bound for hell, staying there for an eon, and incurable.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma.

He holds the view that it is non-Dhamma, yet he is uncertain about the schism; setting aside his view, setting aside his approval, setting aside his preference, and setting aside his disposition, he makes the proclamation and distributes voting tickets.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
Upāli, such a person is also a schismatic of the Saṅgha, bound for a state of misery, destined for hell, remaining there for an eon, and beyond remedy.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu proclaims what is not Dhamma as Dhamma.

He has the view that it is Dhamma regarding that [matter], but the view that it is non-Dhamma regarding the schism … [and so on] … he has the view that it is Dhamma regarding that, and the view that it is Dhamma regarding the schism.
He has the view that it is Dhamma regarding that, but is uncertain regarding the schism.
Being doubtful about that schism, he holds a wrong view regarding it.
Being doubtful about that schism, he holds a right view regarding it.

Being doubtful about that schism, while being himself doubtful, he proclaims the matter and distributes voting tickets, having set aside his own view, having set aside his approval, having set aside his preference, and having set aside his disposition.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
Upāli, such a person is also a schismatic of the Saṅgha, bound for a state of misery, destined for hell, remaining there for an eon, and incurable.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu proclaims what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma... [and so on].”
He proclaims what is not discipline as discipline;
he proclaims discipline as not discipline;
he proclaims what was neither spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims that what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims that what was not practiced by the Tathāgata was practiced by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims that what was practiced by the Tathāgata was not practiced by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as having been laid down by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not having been laid down by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims what is not an offense as an offense.
He proclaims what is an offense as not an offense;
he proclaims a light offense as a heavy offense;
he proclaims a heavy offense as a light offense.
He explains a remainderable offense as a non-remainderable offense;
he explains a non-remainderable offense as a remainderable offense;
he explains a grave offense as a non-grave offense.
He proclaims a non-gross offense as a gross offense … he holds a view of what is not Dhamma regarding that [offense],
and a view of what is not Dhamma regarding the schism … [and so on] … he holds a view of what is not Dhamma regarding that [offense], but a view of what is Dhamma regarding the schism.
In that case, one holds a view of what is not Dhamma regarding the schism, while being doubtful about the schism itself;
or one holds a view of what is Dhamma regarding the schism, while holding a view of what is not Dhamma regarding the schism itself;
or one holds a view of what is Dhamma regarding the schism, while holding a view of what is Dhamma regarding the schism itself.
One who has the view that it is *dhamma* regarding that [matter], but is doubtful regarding the schism;
one who is doubtful regarding that [matter], but has the view that it is *adhamma* regarding the schism;
one who is doubtful regarding that [matter], but has the view that it is *dhamma* regarding the schism.

If one who is doubtful about that [matter], doubtful about the schism, sets aside his view, sets aside his preference, sets aside his inclination, and sets aside his disposition, and then makes the proclamation and distributes the voting tickets, saying:
"This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction;
accept this, approve of this"—Upāli, such a person is also a schismatic of the Saṅgha, bound for a state of misery, destined for hell, staying there for an eon, and beyond remedy.
“But who, venerable sir, is a schismatic who is not destined for the states of deprivation, not destined for hell, not staying there for an eon, and not incurable?
“Here, Upāli, a monk proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma.

Regarding that, he has the view that it is Dhamma; regarding the schism, he has the view that it is Dhamma. Without misrepresenting his view, without misrepresenting his approval, without misrepresenting his preference, and without misrepresenting his disposition, he makes the proclamation and distributes voting tickets.”
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve of this.

Upāli, such a person who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is not one bound for the states of misery, not one bound for hell, not one who remains there for an eon, and not one whose condition is incurable.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu proclaims what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma... [and so on].”
He proclaims a grave offense as a non-grave offense.

He holds the view that it is Dhamma in that matter; he holds the view that it is Dhamma regarding the schism. Without misrepresenting his view, without misrepresenting his acceptance, without misrepresenting his preference, and without misrepresenting his disposition, he makes a proclamation and distributes voting tickets, saying:
"This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this."
"Upāli, this schismatic of the Saṅgha as well is not one bound for the states of misery, not one bound for hell, not one who remains for an eon, and not one beyond remedy.
The third section for recitation is finished.
The seventh chapter on Schismatics of the Saṅgha is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Anupiye, Abhiññātā,
Sukhumālo, Na icchati.
The leeches, the slugs, the flies,
and the maggots; the heaps of chaff and the straw.
Even when their food is scattered on the ground, their fathers and grandfathers do not fail to partake, even from afar.
Bhaddiya and Anuruddha,
Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila,
and Sakyamāna [went] to Kosambī.
And with Kakudha,
he proclaimed to his father the story of the elephant Nāḷāgiri.
Indeed, by three and five grave offenses, one destroys [the Saṅgha]; by a thullaccaya,
and again by three, eight, and three.
"Could there be a schism in the line?
The Sanghabhedakakkhandhaka is concluded.
